newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir crew to study film before rehearsing repair.
newsitem.headline: Mir crew to study film before rehearsing repair.

text.p: The crew of Russia's damaged Mir space station will on Monday study a training film shot on Earth before attempting a risky and complex repair job at the end of the week.

Mission director Vladimir Solovyov told reporters at Korolyov Mission Control, near Moscow, that the two Russian cosmonauts who will do the work and their colleague from NASA would be sent the film during a television link-up on Monday.

The video, shot by fellow cosmonauts wearing bulky space suits in a swimming pool mock-up of the cramped 11-year-old station, will be studied by the crew before a planned six-hour dress rehearsal on Mir on Tuesday.

British-born astronaut Michale Foale, who will take to the station's Soyuz escape capsule during the job on Thursday or Friday night, will be on hand to help his Russian colleagues during Tuesday's practice session, Solovyov said.

Mir commander Vasily Tsibliyev and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin have completed preparing their spacesuits for the sortie into the holed Spektr module to reconnect electric cables and restore power from the module's solar panels.

A collision on June 25 with an unmanned cargo vessel punched a small hole in the module. It was Mir's worst accident and only rapid reactions allowed the crew to seal off the Spektr as air escaped through the hole. But closing the hatches also meant cutting off up to half of Mir's power supply.

A Progress cargo vessel brought repair tools and other vital supplies to Mir a week ago and the crew have now finished unloading it. Among the supplies was equipment to improve communications, making it easier for the cosmonauts to view the training film and stay in contact with Earth during the repairs.
The precise time of the operation will be decided after Tuesday's dress rehearsal, Solovyov said. The cosmonauts will have a rest day before attempting the hazardous repairs.
He said all three men would abandon ship aboard the Soyuz "lifeboat" if things went wrong.
"If a critical situation arises during this work, various options have been considered for an immediate return of all three cosmonauts to Earth," he said.

Solovyov said the Russian Space Agency, which has relied largely on foreign cooperation to keep Mir running during the post-Soviet economic crisis, hopes eventually to make the airless Spektr functional again. A relief crew due to leave in three weeks has been training to find and patch the puncture.
"We are interested in bringing the Spektr module back to life," he said.
